source.title: Monet: Mixture of Monosemantic Experts for Transformers
source.authors: Jungwoo Park; Youngjin Ahn; Kee-Eung Kim; Jaewoo Kang

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses SAE reconstruction errors and evaluates SAE reconstructions on benchmarks, but does not measure the claim’s error structure, predictable scaling, matched-size random-error comparison, or other specified versions.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates Gemma 2 with two SAE reconstruction variants and reports reduced performance qualitatively. Table 2’s flattened layout does not support confidently assigning its benchmark values to those variants, so no numeric values are extracted. Domain masking with Gemma Scope suppresses SAE features rather than measuring SAE reconstruction error; those results are excluded.
record.test_reason: Mainly an architecture paper, but Table 12 reports a usable V5 result. In its SAE-based domain-unlearning baseline, splicing the Gemma Scope SAE into Gemma 2 with no features suppressed drops MMLU by about 3.9 points on average versus the unmodified model. The authors attribute the broader degradation to incomplete reconstruction. That is a feature-steering analysis losing behaviour when the error term is not kept. Nothing bears on V1, V2, V4 or V6, and Table 2 lacks the random-error control V3 needs.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue that post-hoc SAE reconstruction loss compromises performance and stability. They propose MONET, which builds sparse dictionary learning into end-to-end MoE pretraining. They also claim MONET allows domain, language and toxicity unlearning without degrading general performance.
record.recipe_differences: MONET is an end-to-end mixture-of-experts architecture with composed experts, not a post-hoc SAE error analysis or reproduction of the original method.

fits_no_version.finding: Splicing Gemma Scope 65K MLP or residual SAEs into Gemma 2 2B reduces open-ended benchmark performance. The residual SAE appears to fall to near chance on some tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Replacing activations with SAE reconstructions degrades downstream benchmark accuracy, without any random-error comparison.

record.problems: The paper gives a qualitative claim of reduced performance for SAE reconstructions, but the flattened Table 2 values cannot be reliably assigned to the SAE variants here. It does not report a matched-size random-error control or direct measurements of SAE error structure.
record.rows_left_out: Gemma Scope domain-masking results in Figure 3 and Table 12 suppress SAE features rather than measuring reconstruction error, so they were left out.

untested.parts: No linear prediction of SAE error from activations.
No per-token error norms, cross-size comparison or scaling of error.
No comparison of SAE-splice loss against random errors of the same norm.
No split of the error into linear and nonlinear parts.
Circuit analyses are not tested, and the effect is not measured with the error term added back during suppression. Only feature suppression (unlearning) in a single SAE and model is covered.
The paper argues that end-to-end training avoids post-hoc reconstruction loss. But MONET is not an SAE and no dark matter is measured, so whether dark matter is a training artifact is not tested.

missing.what: MMLU accuracy per domain for Gemma 2 2B with the Gemma Scope SAE spliced in and no features suppressed ('None' column), versus without the SAE ('w/o SAE' column). The mean change is about -3.91 points, e.g. Business 63.91 to 55.57 and Psychology 52.81 to 46.75. This is wrongly excluded in rows_left_out: the 'None' column involves no suppression and isolates the cost of reconstruction error.
missing.locator: Appendix E, Table 12; Section 5.1 text on 'incomplete reconstruction through the SAE layer'

record.verdict_notes: The link to V5 is indirect: the SAE is a baseline for knowledge editing, not the object of study. The 'None' column of Table 12 is effectively a with-versus-without-error comparison, but only one model and SAE are covered. The Table 2 values are flattened, so the column assignments above are tentative.

versions.untested_parts: No linear predictability of SAE error from input activations is measured.
No per-token error norms, cross-size predictability, context overlap, or error persistence with scale is measured.
The paper reports benchmark performance with SAE reconstructions, but does not compare against random errors of the same size.
No distinction between linear and nonlinear error components, or their relation to feature learning, is tested.
No circuits or steering analysis compares results with and without the SAE error term.
The paper discusses post-hoc SAE limitations and proposes end-to-end training, but does not test whether dark matter is mostly a training artifact or shrinks under improved SAE training.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated with a 65K-feature SAE reconstructing the LLM’s MLP output.
rows.baseline: Gemma 2 2B without SAE; exact benchmark values not stated in the extractable text
rows.value: Authors state that SAEs fall short in maintaining model stability, with reconstruction errors leading to instability and reduced performance in open-ended tasks.
rows.note: The paper reports the qualitative reduction but Table 2’s flattened layout does not permit reliable assignment of its numeric benchmark values to this SAE row. No random-error comparison is reported, so this does not test V3’s stated comparison.
rows.check: Plain degradation from splicing an SAE, with no matched-size random-error control, so it cannot test V3. The state 'partial' has no version to refer to. The flattened Table 2 is partly readable: the PIQA-like column reads Gemma 0.792 and +SAE MLP 0.723; the final column, likely Avg, reads 0.571 and 0.473. This column assignment is uncertain.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated with a 65K-feature SAE reconstructing residual layers.
rows.baseline: Gemma 2 2B without SAE; exact benchmark values not stated in the extractable text
rows.value: Authors state that SAEs fall short in maintaining model stability, with reconstruction errors leading to instability and reduced performance in open-ended tasks.
rows.note: The paper reports the qualitative reduction but Table 2’s flattened layout does not permit reliable assignment of its numeric benchmark values to this SAE row. No random-error comparison is reported, so this does not test V3’s stated comparison.
rows.check: Same issue as r1: no random-error control. On the same uncertain reading, +SAE Res reads 0.506 on the PIQA-like column (near chance) and 0.337 on the final column, versus Gemma 0.792 and 0.571.

relationships.condition: Gemma 2 2B with Gemma Scope SAE, MMLU domain-unlearning analysis
relationships.reason: Text-based, since no row exists (see missing). Table 12 shows SAE splice with no suppression lowers MMLU in every domain versus no SAE, e.g. History 47.38 to 40.58. The authors blame incomplete reconstruction.
relationships.display_finding: Inserting the SAE without suppressing features reduced MMLU accuracy in every domain, including History from 47.38 to 40.58, which the authors attributed to incomplete reconstruction.
